title: US Revokes More Than 6,000 Visas Linked to Birth Tourism
excerpt: The State Department's Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force passed 6,000 revocations, up from 4,000 at the end of October — targeting travellers and the commercial networks that arranged their trips.
body:
• The US State Department says its Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force has now revoked more than 6,000 visas from people it says engaged in or facilitated birth tourism.
  • The figure is up from the more than 4,000 revocations announced on October 31; the task force was set up on August 12, when the count stood at more than 600.
  • A revocation is not a deportation or a criminal conviction — but a revoked B visitor visa cannot be used to travel, and future applications face the department's rule that travel mainly to give birth for US citizenship is not a valid basis for a B visa.
  • For Indian families: legitimate medical travel remains possible, but applicants must show the treatment purpose honestly — concealing a plan to give birth is what the enforcement targets.

The US State Department said on Thursday that it has revoked more than 6,000 visas from foreigners it says engaged in or facilitated birth tourism, the practice of travelling to the United States mainly to give birth so the child acquires US citizenship. "The Department of State's Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force has now revoked more than 6,000 visas from foreigners who engaged in or facilitated birth tourism," the department said in a post on its official X account, reported by BizzBuzz and IANS. "We are identifying and holding accountable everyone involved in this illicit practice."

How the count climbed

The department established the Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force on August 12, 2026, saying at the time that it had already revoked more than 600 visas globally. On September 23, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced visa restrictions targeting people who knowingly engage in or facilitate birth tourism, with certain family members also potentially covered, and the department opened an online visa-fraud tip portal. By October 31, the department said the revocation total had passed 4,000, including more than 700 visas held by Chinese nationals. The latest statement gave no nationality breakdown, and because each figure was announced as a threshold — "more than" — the exact increase between announcements cannot be calculated.

The rule underneath

The enforcement rests on a State Department rule in place since January 2020. Under that rule, travel "with the primary purpose of obtaining US citizenship for a child by giving birth in the United States is an impermissible basis for the issuance of a B nonimmigrant visa." The rule creates a rebuttable presumption: if a consular officer has reason to believe an applicant will give birth during her stay, the officer may treat birth tourism as the presumed purpose unless the applicant shows a legitimate reason for travel. The rule did not change how US citizenship is acquired — children born in the United States are citizens under the Fourteenth Amendment, a separate legal question that remains in litigation in other contexts.

What a revocation does — and does not — mean

A visa revocation cancels the visa; it does not by itself establish that a person was deported or convicted of a crime, as the reporting on the announcement notes. Birth tourism itself is not a standalone criminal offence, but related conduct — visa fraud, misrepresentation at the interview, or unpaid medical bills arranged through commercial operators — is what investigators have pursued in past cases. The task force model targets the commercial networks that advertise delivery packages, accommodation and coaching, as well as the travellers who used them.

What this means for Indian applicants

India is one of the largest sources of B1/B2 applicants, and pregnancy-related travel questions are already a sensitive part of consular interviews. The practical line the department draws is between concealment and disclosure: travelling for genuine medical treatment, declared honestly with evidence of the treatment plan and ability to pay, is treated differently from travelling with an undisclosed plan to give birth. Applicants who are pregnant or planning medical travel should answer interview questions directly, carry documentation of the medical purpose, and avoid commercial "birth package" operators entirely — association with a facilitator is itself a stated ground for revocation and for the September restrictions, which can extend to family members.

The department has not said how many of the 6,000-plus revoked visas were held by Indian nationals, and it has not published a country-by-country breakdown for the latest total.
nri_angle: Indian B1/B2 applicants face direct questions on pregnancy-related travel; the line enforcement draws is disclosure versus concealment of a plan to give birth.
